FRONT / story / draft
2 trees: Build your (D)Home
One small chainsaw. One hundred and twenty wedge members. Forty
triangles. Two weeks to attempt a frame.
A practical explanation and a builder's field story, beginning with two trees
and following the decisions that turn them into a geodesic dome.
This is the working manuscript. The construction described here is a
planned build; its outcome will be recorded as it happens. The author
describes the intended saw as a Husqvarna 120 Mark III purchased from
Lowe's. The exact product label, receipt, and supplied bar-and-chain
combination belong in the equipment record before publication.

pages.title: Before the first chapter
pages.text:
FRONT / reference / draft
Before the first chapter
There are three ways to read this book. Follow the story to understand how
the idea arrived. Follow the explanation to understand why the geometry
works. Follow the how-to pages to organize measurements, prototypes,
material, and assembly. Each chapter has a strand so that a reader can
change pace without losing their place.
The title sets the scale of the experiment. Two trees are the intended source
of the frame's wedge members. They do not include the ground connection,
fasteners, seam components, skin, services, or everything required for a
dwelling. The fortnight is a target for making and framing the dome, with
its preparation stated openly. Occupancy is a later milestone with its own
requirements.
The book uses A for the long chord and B for the short chord. Other
references may reverse these letters. Compare lengths and factors before
comparing names. Dimensions are inches unless marked feet; trunk
diameter always means a measurement across the trunk, not the radius.
The number printed beside an ideal triangle is not automatically a saw cut.
We will follow that distinction from the first sketch to the last stock check.
A blank is the piece available to fabricate a member. A member is the
finished wooden part. An edge is a line in the mathematical mesh. A seam
is the interface between neighboring panels. Confusing these words is an
easy way to build the right arithmetic into the wrong object.
The geometry in this draft traces to the project files listed in the source
appendix. Practical prescriptions for structural connections must be
supported by an appropriate design for the actual site and timber. The
simulator establishes shape and fit; it does not establish allowable loads.
This boundary is part of describing the project accurately.

pages.title: Part I — The idea in the wood
pages.text:
PART / story / draft
Part I — The idea in the
wood
Before a cut list, there was a question: what if the useful shape was already
inside the tree?
We begin with the earlier experiments, then arrive at the wedge. This part
explains the discovery without pretending that every later detail was
obvious at the beginning.

pages.title: 1. Start with what is here
pages.text:
CHAPTER / story / draft
1. Start with what is here
I want to find out how directly I can get from a tree to a frame. Not from a
stack of uniform lumber, not from a kit delivered with every decision
already made, but from the wood itself. The shape of that wood has to enter
the design early enough to matter.
The proposal is small enough to count. Forty triangular frames need three
members each: one hundred and twenty members. Two suitable trunks,
each divided into eight useful sections, could yield eight wedge blanks per
section. That is sixty-four blanks from each tree, sixty intended members
and four potential spares. Those are the starting numbers, before I know
which pieces the wood will actually permit.
The time limit gives the question an edge. I intend to design, produce the
members, and frame the dome within two weeks, using the small
Husqvarna saw described in my equipment notes. A limited tool makes the
length and repeatability of the parts important. The saw's role belongs in
the story because it affects the process; its model name is not a
performance guarantee.
There is a temptation to tell the ending first. A photograph of a finished
dome would make the early uncertainty disappear. I want to keep that
uncertainty visible. Where does a nominal six-foot dimension become a
real part? How much straight trunk is there after defects and cut losses?
Which joint detail survives a full-size trial? Those questions are what the
build is for.
The first record will be the starting inventory. Photograph both source
trunks or the available sections. Include a tape in the frame. Record the
actual usable lengths, the smallest diameters, and every assumption used to
choose the initial dome. If the available wood changes the plan, the change
becomes a chapter in the experiment.

pages.title: 2. What the Frankendome taught me
pages.text:
CHAPTER / story / draft
2. What the Frankendome
taught me
The earlier project notes describe the Frankendome as an experiment in
joining unlike triangular frames. Its members were deliberately varied. The
problem was not only how to make a triangle, but how one completed
triangle could meet another when their edges did not offer identical
profiles.
That experiment made the interface important. The notes describe testing
V brackets at edge-to-edge and corner relationships. A connector that can
accommodate an awkward member is useful because it lets the designer
ask what the material can do before demanding that every piece become
conventional rectangular lumber.
The notes also describe a modified upper pentagon: ten pieces in that
earlier configuration where another arrangement would use fifteen. That
number belongs to the earlier experiment. It must not quietly replace the
forty-face, one-hundred-and-twenty-member count used for the book's
standard panelized 2V hemisphere. A prototype can teach the next design
without being the same design.
The useful inheritance is a way of thinking. Build manageable units. Give
each unit a defined boundary. Study what happens at that boundary. If the
connector and the member profile are designed together, the member has
more possible shapes than the lumber aisle suggests.
For the final story, place the earliest dated Frankendome photograph
beside a later wedge prototype. Describe one specific connection that was
troublesome, what was tried, and what it revealed. The present draft has
the sequence from the project notes; it still needs the author's remembered
scene and the evidence that anchors it.

pages.title: 3. Finding the wedge
pages.text:
CHAPTER / story / draft
3. Finding the wedge
A round trunk contains eight equal radial sectors if its cross-section is
divided at forty-five-degree intervals. Extend one sector along a straight
section of trunk and it becomes a long member with two sawn radial faces
and the original curved outside. The curve that rectangular milling would
remove becomes part of the proposed frame.
The discovery in the project notes is the relationship between this profile
and a panelized dome. A small triangular frame provides a repeatable use
for the wedge. A separate seam detail can accommodate how neighboring
triangles turn relative to one another. The member no longer has to do
every geometric job by itself.
This is also where the attractive claims need to become questions.
Preserving the curved portion can preserve material, but an area
calculation alone does not say how much usable framing emerges from a
real tree. The bark, defects, taper, irregular saw path, and the ends of the
member still matter. The useful discovery is a method worth measuring,
not a percentage protected from measurement.
In the design software, the wedge can face in four cardinal directions. Its
point can face into the dome, out toward the sky, into its own triangular
panel, or across the panel boundary. Each orientation changes the
relationships at the seams and corners. The original outward-curve
description is one configuration of the larger investigation.
The book's most useful discovery scene will show a change in
understanding. Preserve a sketch or photograph of the first wedge beside
the first assembled corner. Record what the wood suggested, what the
model corrected, and what the full-size piece later changed again. Those
three moments give the explanation a human sequence.

pages.title: 4. Define the experiment before starting the clock
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
4. Define the experiment
before starting the clock
Write the finish line in a sentence that someone else could check: produce
and assemble the selected dome frame from documented source timber.
Define which preparatory work happens before day one. Existing software
development, drawings, fixtures, equipment purchases, site preparation,
and professional design work may all be real contributions even when the
cutting-and-framing clock has not started.
Use four milestone records: material available; accepted members
produced; triangular panels checked; frame assembled and inspected
against its design. A pile of ripped wedges reaches the first fabrication
milestone. A standing frame reaches another. Neither should be counted as
a finished home.
Keep an equipment ledger. The planned saw is identified by the author as a
Husqvarna 120 Mark III from Lowe's. Record the nameplate and actual
configuration rather than copying specifications from another generation
of the 120. The manufacturer uses product-number information to
distinguish variants; the purchase record resolves the particular machine in
this story. Husqvarna product identification
(https://us-support.husqvarna.com/en/petrol-chainsaw/KA-70145).
Also record the other work required to make the saw useful: measuring,
securing and supporting work, moving timber, maintaining the tool,
marking members, making fixtures, and managing the site. A small saw
does not make those operations disappear. It makes the organization
around them especially visible.
Before field work, use training appropriate to the operations and the
manufacturer's instructions for the exact equipment. Protective equipment,
secure work support, separation from helpers, and emergency

pages.title: Part II — The dome before the saw
pages.text:
PART / explanation / draft
Part II — The dome before
the saw
A sphere can be imagined continuously. Wood must arrive as countable
pieces.
This part takes the project from a radius to a mesh, then from a mesh to
independent wooden panels. Keep the reference geometry visible while the
physical object becomes more complicated.

pages.title: 5. A sphere made from straight lines
pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
5. A sphere made from
straight lines
A geodesic construction begins with a regular organization of directions on
a sphere. In this project's 2V model, the triangular faces of an icosahedron
are subdivided once and the resulting points are projected to the sphere.
The chords between those projected points become the straight edges of the
triangulation.
The frequency describes subdivision. It does not say how many feet across
the dome is. A 2V dome can be enlarged or reduced while retaining its
geometric relationships. Every nominal edge scales with the sphere radius,
which is why a dimensionless chord factor can connect a desired dome size
to a length on the bench.
The hemisphere used here contains forty triangular faces, twenty-six
vertices, and sixty-five unique edges. Its open rim is a ten-sided polygon.
The vertices on that rim lie on a circle; the floor boundary between them is
made from straight lines. This difference matters when quoting floor area.
The model separates two edge classes. With the book's lettering, A is the
longer chord and B is the shorter. Ten panels have three A sides. Thirty
panels have one A side and two B sides. The corresponding triangle shapes
repeat, but the real wooden members also depend on how their corners and
seams are made.
Look at the topology plate before the timber plate. In the topology, a line
has no thickness, no end cut, and no fastener. Its value is precision: it
establishes exactly what the assembly is meant to follow. The wooden
model adds the decisions necessary to occupy space around those lines.

6. Why 65 edges need 120
pieces of wood
The dome's shared-edge mesh and its independent-panel frame count
different things. If each mathematical edge owned one stick, the
hemisphere would use sixty-five sticks. In this project, each of forty
triangles owns all three of its wooden members. The frame therefore
contains 40 × 3 = 120 members.

Two neighboring triangles bring two pieces of wood to their common
boundary. The duplication is intentional. Each triangular unit can be made
and checked before it joins the dome. The space between its member and
the neighboring panel's member becomes the seam detail.
Of the sixty-five unique mesh edges, ten are at the exposed base rim and
fifty-five lie between two panels. Count forty panels × three edges to get one
hundred and twenty panel-edge incidences. Count the same incidences
another way: fifty-five interior edges appear twice and ten boundary edges
appear once. Thus 55 × 2 + 10 = 120.
There are thirty-five long edges and thirty short edges in the unique-edge
mesh. Ten of the long edges are on the base. The shared seams are
therefore twenty-five long and thirty short. Use the member count to plan
wedge stock; use the seam count to plan panel interfaces. Hardware
quantities require the selected detail at each interface and cannot be
inferred by calling all edges “struts.”

pages.title: 7. Method one: start with the radius you want
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
7. Method one: start with the
radius you want
Choose a sphere radius R, then keep one unit throughout the calculation. If
the radius is in feet and the working dimensions will be inches, multiply it
by twelve before finding the chords.
The nominal relationships are A = R × fA and B = R × fB. For this project's
exact generated 2V mesh, fA is approximately 0.618033989 and fB is
approximately 0.546533058. The Sizing lab obtains these factors from the
existing geometry module rather than keeping the rounded printed values
as its authority.
The procedure is sequential. Record the desired radius. Generate both
chord lengths. Confirm the forty-panel inventory. Select the member
cross-section, orientation, and seam construction. Generate the physical
model and inspect its actual stock lengths. Only then select raw blank
lengths and allocate trees.
If a radius gives nominal edges that are inconvenient for the timber, the
design still has options. A slightly smaller radius can reduce length
demand. A different seam or corner setting can change the stock envelope.
More usable source length may be available in a longer section. Each option
must be checked through the same solver; none should be hidden inside an
unexplained rounding choice.
Record three lengths for each member: the ideal chord, the finished
physical stock envelope, and the blank required to fabricate it. The last
includes whatever additional holding, trimming, and overfit stock the
actual process needs. Zero extra allowance in the lab explicitly means that
only the finished envelope is being checked.
When the stock plan is complete, export the actual simulator's bill of
materials and cut schedule for the chosen configuration. The book can

pages.text:
explain the reasoning, while that schedule preserves the geometry used for
the build. Write the configuration and date beside any printed schedule so
an older paper does not silently govern a newer design.

pages.title: 8. Worked example: a ten-foot radius
pages.text:
WORKED / explanation / draft
8. Worked example: a
ten-foot radius
Use a sphere radius of 10 feet, or 120 inches. The nominal diameter is 20
feet. Multiply the exact mesh factors by 120 to obtain a long chord of
approximately 74.164 inches and a short chord of approximately 65.584
inches.
The panelized frame requires sixty members associated with A edges and
sixty associated with B edges. These labels identify edge families, not
necessarily just two physical cut lengths. A member's surrounding triangle
and joint relationships can split a nominal family into multiple fabrication
cases.
The enclosing base circle has area π × 10², approximately 314.159 square
feet. The straight-sided decagonal base has area 5 × 10² × sin(36°),
approximately 293.893 square feet. Neither quantity is the finished usable
floor area after wall build-up, foundations, doors, and fittings. The circle is
a useful reference; the polygon describes this mesh's base.
For a concrete physical comparison, the current raw-wedge solver with an
eight-inch trunk diameter, point facing into the dome, raw-trapezoid
seams, and no additional fabrication allowance produces a longest finished
stock envelope of approximately 72.952 inches at this radius. That is
different from the 74.164-inch nominal A chord because the member's
actual ends and offsets are solved separately.
This example reveals why a six-foot blank cannot simply be assigned to a
“six-foot dome edge,” and why the error does not always have the same
sign. Some physical parts are shorter than the nominal edge; different
settings and additional holding stock can change what the blank must
provide. Inspect the physical schedule instead of assuming a fixed
deduction.

pages.title: 9. Method two: let the tree set the size
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
9. Method two: let the tree
set the size
Begin with a measured inventory rather than a desired radius. Identify
usable straight sections in the available trunks. Record their lengths, their
smaller-end diameters, and the defects that affect where a member can be
obtained. A tall tree and a long run of usable stock are different
measurements.
The book's starting proposal is eight sections of approximately six feet from
each tree. Eight radial blanks per section produce 8 × 8 = 64 potential
blanks from one tree. Reserving four for rejection or spares leaves sixty
intended members. Two trees produce 128 potential blanks and a target
allocation of 120 members.
This is a count-based first pass. A blank earns its place in the frame only
after it meets the length, cross-section, straightness, and material
requirements for its assigned part. Eight adequate pieces at the butt of the
tree do not prove that eight adequate pieces also exist in every upper
section.
Let S be the usable blank length after planned end trimming. A
nominal-only starting estimate is R = S / fA. If S is 72 inches, that gives a
radius of approximately 116.498 inches, or 9.708 feet, and a diameter of
approximately 19.416 feet. The corresponding nominal short chord is about
63.670 inches.
That estimate intentionally ignores physical corner and seam geometry. To
size the real frame, hold the selected cross-section and joint settings fixed
and solve for the largest radius whose every required blank fits the
available length. The Sizing lab's “Fit physical stock” action uses the
raw-wedge solver for this check. Enter any additional fabrication stock

pages.title: 9. Method two: let the tree set the size
pages.text:
rather than treating the final installed piece as the whole blank
requirement.
The two methods meet here. Design-first asks how much wood a chosen
radius requires. Tree-first asks what radius the available wood permits.
With identical joint settings and allowances, going forward and then
backward should return the same design. That round trip is an unusually
useful check on a cut list.

cross-sections as wedges are produced. Both matter, but subtracting one
from the other would mix different dimensions.

pages.title: Part III — The tree becomes inventory
pages.text:
PART / explanation / draft
Part III — The tree becomes
inventory
The model contains ideal circles. The source timber contains taper, history,
and surprises.
This part turns the attractive gross count into a traceable inventory of
usable pieces. The small section is valuable because each decision can be
local, visible, and recorded.

pages.title: 11. The shape of one eighth
pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
11. The shape of one eighth
For a circular trunk of radius r, one ideal eighth-sector has an angle of 45
degrees and area πr²/8. Its two radial sides each have length r. The outside
is an arc, not a straight third side. Its arc length is πr/4; the straight chord
joining the arc's endpoints is 2r sin(22.5°).
For an eight-inch diameter trunk, r is four inches. The ideal sector area is
approximately 6.283 square inches. The curved arc is approximately 3.142
inches long, while its straight chord is approximately 3.061 inches. These
describe a raw circular sector before kerf, bark removal, or other changes.
Drawing a triangle in its place removes some of the wood the idea is trying
to preserve.
For a twelve-inch diameter trunk, the ideal sector area grows to
approximately 14.137 square inches. A six-foot length of that ideal sector
contains about 1,017.9 cubic inches, or 7.07 solid-volume board feet. Board
feet here are only a volume unit: 144 cubic inches per board foot. This
calculation is not a lumber grade or a market valuation.
A wedge can have substantial area while still presenting difficult bearing
surfaces and connections. Its orientation changes how it occupies the panel
boundary. Its taper changes the section along its length. Its grain and
defects change the material that carries load. The book therefore uses the
cross-section to explain the shape and the inventory, while keeping
strength evaluation attached to the actual member and design.
The illustration on this page should show a whole log cross-section beside
one true sector, then the same sector oriented in the four ways explored by
the simulator. Use end-grain views. A long perspective drawing can hide
the very profile the reader needs to understand.

pages.title: 12. Read the trunk in sections
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
12. Read the trunk in
sections
Give each source tree an ID before allocating members. Give each
candidate section a second ID and mark its original orientation. Then
record usable length, large-end diameter, small-end diameter, visible
sweep, knots, checks, damage, and any reason a region must be excluded.
Photograph the section beside its label.
A short-section method can respond to local curvature. If a bend interrupts
a long run, the useful material on either side may still supply shorter
members. This is a possibility to inspect, not a guarantee that any crooked
trunk can be converted into the planned stock count. Every new boundary
also consumes length through a cut and may create an end that needs
trimming.
Use the smallest relevant cross-section when checking whether a blank
provides the material the design requires throughout its length. An
impressive butt diameter is not the diameter of an upper six-foot section. A
circular model also needs to be reconciled with an oval or irregular real
section before its area becomes an inventory claim.
Make assignments provisionally. A long, sound blank can remain
uncommitted until the most demanding members are covered. Shorter
acceptable blanks can be considered for the B family. Pieces awaiting
judgment should stay in a separate recorded category so that uncertain
stock does not appear in the accepted count.
The field ledger is more useful than a single yield percentage. Its rows can
answer where a missing member went. Was it lost to end damage, excessive
taper, a defect exposed during cutting, or a fabrication error? Those
explanations turn an experiment into a process another person can
evaluate.

pages.title: 13. Measure recovery instead of defending a percentage
pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
13. Measure recovery
instead of defending a
percentage
The discovery notes propose a high wood recovery and compare it with
conventional milling. That is a useful hypothesis. To test it, define the
numerator and denominator before looking at the result. Gross solid trunk
volume, sawn sector volume, accepted member volume, and installed
member volume are different quantities.
For a simplified circular section, the total kerf area of four diametral cut
planes can be estimated by 4Dk, where D is diameter and k is kerf width.
Compared with the round area πD²/4, the simple retained fraction is
approximately 1 - 16k/(πD). The approximation ignores overlaps between
cut bands near the center and assumes the intended cut geometry. Actual
kerf paths, bark, irregular shape, end losses, and rejected wood change the
result.
At D = 12 inches and k = 0.25 inch, this simple estimate retains
approximately 89.39 percent before those other losses. At D = 8 inches
with the same kerf assumption, it retains approximately 84.08 percent. The
change with diameter is enough to show why one attractive percentage
should not stand in for an entire tapered tree.
The earlier project timber model computes a tapered trunk by sections and
compares its wedge output with its own rectangular packing model. Record
that comparison's assumptions: section length, kerf, taper, nominal or
actual rectangular dimensions, and acceptance criteria. A result for true
two-by-fours is not automatically a result for dressed nominal
two-by-fours.

pages.title: 13. Measure recovery instead of defending a percentage
pages.text:
The book's final comparison should use the same starting inventory on
both sides. Include labor, equipment, defects, and the material that
genuinely replaces a required product. A wedge with more volume than a
rectangular stick is not automatically worth that volume multiplied by a
store price. It must perform the intended job through an appropriate
design.
The author can make the strongest account by keeping the unfriendly rows:
pieces rejected, setup that took longer, and usable stock left over. Those
rows show where the method can improve and prevent a gross-material
argument from pretending to be a finished-building argument.

pages.title: 14. Wood keeps changing after the cut
pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
14. Wood keeps changing
after the cut
The model's geometry stays still after a calculation. Freshly cut timber
continues to exchange moisture with its surroundings. Changes in
dimensions, shape, and checking can affect joints that fitted at the first
assembly. The field record therefore needs dates and moisture
observations, not just a photograph of a tight new corner.
Record the timber species when it is reliably identified, the condition of the
stock, how it was stored, and any moisture readings with the method used.
Preserve examples of the cross-section at fabrication and at later
inspection. When a seam changes, this record helps distinguish an initial
cutting error from movement after assembly.
The USDA Wood Handbook organizes moisture relations, mechanical
properties, fastenings, grading, and drying as separate but related subjects.
Those are the subjects the prototype's material record needs to connect.
USDA Wood Handbook
(https://research.fs.usda.gov/fpl/wood-handbook).
Avoid turning an attractive green-wood fit into a prediction of long-term
performance. The final fastening and seam design needs to account for the
actual timber, exposure, and changes over time. The two-week schedule
does not erase those later observations; it gives them a clear initial
condition.
Reserve a few documented samples for follow-up. Mark them with the
same tree and section IDs used in the member ledger. If a sample changes
while the frame is in service, it becomes a small, accessible witness to the
larger material process. Its behavior is evidence to interpret, not a
substitute for inspecting the actual frame.

Part IV — One hundred and
twenty useful pieces
Repeatability is the bridge between a promising shape and a buildable set

This part moves from a representative blank to a checked corner, then to a

pages.title: 15. Organize the work around the small saw
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
15. Organize the work
around the small saw
The intended tool is part of the constraint that makes the experiment
interesting. It is also a machine with a defined operating envelope. Record
its actual model, approved equipment combination, condition, and
maintenance. Use its manual and appropriate instruction to determine
operations and setup; do not infer capability from an illustration or from
bar length alone.
The planning sequence begins with stock that has been safely obtained,
supported, and made accessible. Divide the work into measurement and
marking, material processing, inspection, and storage. Give each activity
enough room that an interruption does not put an unmarked or
uninspected member into the accepted stack.
Before committing the inventory, document one representative sample
through the proposed process. Measure the resulting kerf and the usable
piece. Record the time spent securing and repositioning work, maintaining
the chain, and clearing material. Cutting time alone describes only one part
of the operation.
Keep the production log short enough to use. A row needs the source
section, resulting blank IDs, accepted count, rejected count, elapsed labor,
and reason for losses. A photograph of the labeled group supports the row.
If a process change improves the result, label when it started so the book
can compare like with like.
The goal is a controlled batch, not a dramatic image of hurried cutting. The
story can include fatigue, a dull chain, weather, or a setup that had to be
changed if those events occur. They belong in the account because they
explain the labor needed to transform a counted tree into counted parts.

pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
16. Four ways to place the
same wedge
The raw-wedge simulator names each orientation by the direction of the
sector point. Point dome in directs the point toward the sphere center.
Point dome out turns it toward the exterior. Point panel in turns it
toward the center of its own triangular panel. Point panel out directs it
across the panel boundary.
These labels describe cross-section orientation around the member's long
axis. They do not rename the geodesic edge. An A edge remains an A edge
while the wood surrounding it changes position. The change can alter
which face is available for a seam or a neighboring member's end.
Compare all four with identical nominal dome size, trunk diameter, and
seam settings. Use a wide view to see the overall frame and a close
end-grain view to understand the interface. Record the configuration on
the figure rather than relying on a nickname such as “inside-out.”
The project's original specification uses the curved surface toward the sky
and the point inward. Later tools explore the other orientations. The
narrative should make this progression visible: the first idea established a
starting configuration; inspection then opened a larger design space.
Selecting an orientation is a fabrication decision. Once a representative
full-size panel has been checked, mark that orientation on each blank and
in the fixture documentation. A correct length installed with an unintended
quarter-turn is a different physical assembly.

pages.title: 17. The triangle corner is a physical object
pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
17. The triangle corner is a
physical object
The ideal triangle has vertices where lines meet. Real members have width,
depth, and ends that must occupy different space. The project's pinwheel
arrangement gives each member a receiving role at one end and a
terminating role at the other. One member ends against the side of its
neighbor while receiving another member in turn.
Earlier explanatory code describes simplified square-ended pinwheel
members. The current raw-wedge simulator carries more detailed corner
geometry: the terminating end is solved against its receiving surface, and
the other end is clipped to the triangle's envelope. The corresponding cut
planes and stock extents should govern the fabrication discussion for this
configuration.
This correction matters to the story. Preserving the longitudinal
forty-five-degree sector does not imply that every end is a square crosscut.
The long radial faces, the panel-to-panel fold, and the member's end cuts
are separate geometric questions. A process can preserve the raw sector
while still requiring an oblique end cut.
Start with a full-size representative corner using the intended cross-section
and orientation. Mark the mathematical reference points and the actual cut
surfaces separately. Check the receiving relationship, the available bearing
region, the fastening space, and whether either member extends beyond
the intended panel envelope.
Move from that corner to one A-A-A panel and one B-A-B panel. Check
their reference dimensions and their physical boundaries. A fixture that
reproduces one family does not automatically reproduce the other. Before
cutting the batch, retain a labeled master example and the configuration
that produced it.

pages.title: 18. Build the reference into the fixture
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
18. Build the reference into
the fixture
A fixture is a way to make the important measurements repeatable. Begin
with the selected triangle's reference geometry, then establish stops,
registration surfaces, and cut references from the actual physical model.
The fixture should make it clear which part of the irregular wedge is being
located and which remains free to vary.
The simulator's jig stages are useful illustrations because they separate
setup, placement, and trimming. Review them with the chosen model. Do
not transfer a picture's apparent dimension onto wood: use the current cut
schedule and a verified full-size layout.
Write down the allowance used at each end. The model includes concepts
such as head overfit and butt hangoff. Those are deliberately sacrificial
pieces of stock, and their values can make a blank longer than the final
member. A six-foot finished part with additional holding stock requires
more than six feet of raw material.
After the representative panels are assembled, compare them with the
reference layout. Check edge references, corner positions, plane of the
frame, and the surfaces that will meet adjacent panels. Record the
acceptance criteria from the actual design. “Looks triangular” is not a
measurement a second builder can reproduce.
The fixture record should contain an overhead photograph, the version of
the layout, the panel family, the wedge orientation, the stock cross-section
used for the trial, and any adjustments made after the first piece. If a stop
moves during the batch, identify which parts were made before and after
that change.
The fixture is also a storytelling object. It shows the moment the project
becomes a repeatable process. A reader can see how the useful idea was

pages.title: 18. Build the reference into the fixture
pages.text:
transferred from screen to bench, and which details had to change when
the material became real.

pages.title: 19. Make forty triangles, one checked batch at a time
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
19. Make forty triangles, one
checked batch at a time
Build the inventory around two panel families: ten A-A-A frames and thirty
B-A-B frames. Preserve the member IDs through assembly so each
completed panel can be traced to its source sections. A panel label should
identify its family, handedness, orientation, and position in the assembly
plan.
Treat the first checked panel of each family as a reference, not as
permission to stop measuring. Recheck the fixture after adjustments and at
sensible batch intervals. When a piece is rejected, keep the reason in the
log. Reworking it, replacing it, and accepting it unchanged are different
outcomes.
The short family is not simply whatever remains after making long
members. Each B member still needs the right usable section and joint
geometry. Allocate the demanding pieces first, then review how the
remaining inventory can satisfy the rest of the schedule. The source tree
assignment can change while the member's required geometry stays fixed.
At the end of each batch, update three counts: blanks remaining; finished
accepted members; completed accepted panels. This avoids the common
error of counting the same wood once as a member and again as part of a
panel. Keep rejected and experimental material outside those totals.
Photograph completed panels flat from overhead and with a low angle that
reveals their profile. Include a scale reference and a readable label. Those
images serve the book's explanatory pages, but their first job is to
document what was actually built.
Before transport or raising, check the completed inventory against the
assembly map and the design's handling plan. Panels have mass and can be
awkward to control even when each member was manageable alone. The

pages.text:
modular method changes the unit being handled; the handling
arrangements must change with it.

pages.title: Part V — The seams make the dome
pages.text:
PART / how-to / draft
Part V — The seams make
the dome
Forty correct triangles are an inventory. Their connected relationships
make the frame.
The next chapters follow those relationships from the shared seam to the
ground and then to the larger question implied by the word home.

pages.title: 20. What happens between two panels
pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
20. What happens between
two panels
At an interior edge, two outward panel normals point in slightly different
directions. The small angle between them is the fold: F = acos(N1 · N2) for
normalized normals, with the numerical dot product clamped to the valid
range. The internal supplementary angle is 180 degrees minus F. Print the
definition beside the number because “dihedral” is used in different ways.
The raw sector contributes its own fixed face relationships. In the original
point-inward comparison, the ideal residual gap angle is related to 45
degrees minus the panel fold. The actual contact surfaces, offsets, and
selected seam mode must still be solved in their physical positions. An
attractive sketch does not define a fabrication polygon.
The project's seam studies include rigid keys, hose or gasket concepts, and
a shaved-flat alternative. The current raw-trapezoid mode preserves the
longitudinal sector faces and uses a truncated key profile. The shaved-flat
configuration changes those seam faces and uses a different key. These are
distinct construction choices and should have separate captions and
schedules.
A rigid shape can help establish a geometric relationship when the surfaces
meet as intended. A round hose or gasket mainly fills space and can permit
relative rotation unless the connection independently constrains it. Filling
a gap, setting an angle, transferring structural forces, and managing water
are different jobs. A single interface may need several components to do
them.
Make a representative two-panel seam before the larger assembly. Use the
actual timber profiles and the proposed connection detail. Record the fit,
the available fastening geometry, and the relationship to the reference fold.
This trial helps locate a problem while it can still be handled on the bench.

pages.title: 21. Give the frame a place to stand
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
21. Give the frame a place to
stand
The base ring is a ten-sided boundary in the selected hemisphere. It must
be laid out from a consistent center and reference dimensions. A radius
drawn on the ground locates the circumcircle; the segments joining the
base vertices locate the polygon. Record which reference was used at every
check.
The structural path continues from the panels through their connections
and into the support and anchorage system. The base is therefore part of
the design, even though the two trees are supplying the wedge members
above it. Record the actual foundation or support approach, site
information, and the design responsible for uplift, sliding, settlement, and
the applicable loads.
Check the base layout before accepting panel fit as evidence about the
dome. A misplaced support can make correct panels appear wrong. An
improvised adjustment in one seam can then distribute that error through
several others. Keep the layout measurements separate from the panel
acceptance measurements so the source of a mismatch can be found.
The book should include a plan-view plate with base vertex IDs and
reference dimensions from the chosen model. Pair it with an actual site
photograph showing the same labels. This pair is more useful than a
generic rendering because it connects the drawing to the place where the
assembly must close.
Any doorway that interrupts the frame or base changes the local
arrangement. Describe the intended opening as an explicit design variant.
Do not silently remove members from the forty-triangle scheme while
continuing to quote its original topology and stock count.

pages.title: 22. Follow an assembly plan that can stay stable
pages.text:
CHAPTER / how-to / draft
22. Follow an assembly plan
that can stay stable
The assembly order must come from a plan for the actual panels,
connections, equipment, and site. A complete dome's behavior does not
describe an incomplete ring of panels. Temporary support, controlled
handling, and the limits of each intermediate stage need their own
attention.
Before raising begins, lay out the panel map and verify every label against
it. Identify each planned seam, the connection components it requires, and
the stage at which it can be checked. Record where temporary support is
required and what inspection permits a stage to proceed. These details
should be supplied by the build's actual assembly and structural plan.
The earlier Frankendome notes discuss a top-down experiment. That
history belongs in the narrative, but it does not choose the safe order for
this different frame. The present book should show the sequence actually
adopted, with its equipment and supports visible in the photographs.
As the frame grows, compare reference nodes and the base with the model.
A forced seam is useful information. Pause to identify whether the cause is
the base layout, a panel dimension, an orientation error, or a connection
mismatch. Record the diagnosis and correction so the story preserves the
discovery rather than editing out the difficulty.
The closure is an important scene only if its conditions are visible.
Photograph the final relationship before and after connection, record any
adjustment, and retain the final dimensional checks. The reader should be
able to understand what “it fit” meant beyond the relief of seeing the last
piece in place.

pages.title: 23. The frame and the home it might become
pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
23. The frame and the home
it might become
The parenthesis in (D)Home keeps two scales in view. This project is
making a dome frame. The larger ambition is useful shelter shaped by that
frame. The next decisions include the envelope, openings, drainage,
insulation, ventilation, services, interior space, and maintenance access.
The project already explores many of these subjects. Dome Creator can
show frames, panels, interiors, and site arrangements. Other lessons
examine energy, material quantities, assembly flow, and alternative shapes.
Use those tools to illustrate questions the frame creates, while labeling
conceptual configurations so a reader does not mistake an image for a
completed building detail.
The seam has to be considered again when a skin is introduced. Water
follows exterior geometry and discontinuities, not the simplicity of a frame
diagram. An opening introduces edges where layers end or turn. A service
penetration has to be coordinated with the envelope and with the structure.
Those are design topics to develop explicitly in a later phase.
Space also deserves a measured description. The base polygon, the curved
wall profile, and the location of the useful head-height zone influence
furniture and circulation. A floor area quoted from an enclosing circle tells
only part of that story. Include a plan and a section when describing a
proposed interior.
At the fortnight's end, name the achieved milestone precisely. If the frame
is standing, describe that accomplishment and its remaining work. If a
problem has delayed the frame, describe the problem and what the
experiment established. The title can hold ambition without requiring the
field record to invent completion.

pages.title: 25. Count the work the wood actually replaced
pages.text:
CHAPTER / explanation / draft
25. Count the work the wood
actually replaced
The discovery notes use an illustrative store price and a proposed
production rate to ask whether wedge-making can have meaningful value.
Preserve those figures as the origin of the question, with their original date
and uncertainty. Replace them with receipts and measured labor when
making a claim about this build.
Separate cash spent, reusable equipment acquired, consumables used, and
labor hours. A saw bought for this project still has value afterward, while
fuel and oil used during the project do not. A comparison can show either
initial cash requirement or allocated project cost, but it should say which
one it shows.
Count labor from setup through completed accepted parts. Record
maintenance, movement, fixture work, inspection, failed attempts, and
cleanup where they belong. A rate measured during one productive
afternoon does not establish the average rate for the whole frame. The book
can show both the good run and the full ledger.
To compare with purchased lumber, define the product the purchased
material would have supplied. Volume equality alone does not establish
equal structural function, connection cost, dimensional stability, or finish
quality. The strongest comparison is between complete, specified
alternatives that serve the same purpose.
Use the same discipline for the “two trees” claim. It describes the proposed
source of wedge members. List added seam material, fasteners, supports,
and anything bought for the base separately. The extra rows do not weaken
the experiment; they show its actual boundary.
The economic ending can remain useful even if it is mixed. The method
may save a machine while requiring more handling. It may preserve wood

while demanding a more involved connection. Those tradeoffs tell a future
builder where the method fits and where a conventional alternative may fit
better.

pages.title: 26. What two trees will have taught me
pages.text:
CHAPTER / story / draft
26. What two trees will have
taught me
At the beginning, the idea fits in one sentence: use the wedge that a tree
already contains to make the repeated parts of a dome. By the end, that
sentence should have acquired measurements, joints, mistakes,
photographs, and a result.
I want the last chapter to return to the first inventory. How many sections
did the actual trees supply? How many blanks became accepted members?
Which allowance changed after the first physical trial? How much of the
fortnight went into sawing, how much into making the geometry
repeatable, and how much into joining the panels?
Those answers cannot be written in advance. What can be written is the
standard they must meet. The count should reconcile. The final model
should match the built configuration. The photographs should show the
important details. The story should preserve the moments where the wood
or the assembly contradicted the expectation.
If the frame comes together within the target, the account should explain
what preparation and conditions made that possible. If it takes longer, the
account should explain the difference. The discovery has value when
another person can understand and evaluate it; a protected deadline would
make the explanation less useful.
The closing scene belongs to the author after the work. Return to one object
from the opening: a source stump, an unused wedge, the saw, or the first
sketch. Describe it as it is now, after the experiment. Let the measured
result and the lived scene occupy the same page.

pages.title: Glossary — the words beside the cuts
pages.text:
APPENDIX / reference / draft
Glossary — the words beside
the cuts
A / B: This book's long / short nominal geodesic edge families.
Blank: The stock available before a member's final cuts, including
necessary process allowance.
Chord factor: The ratio of an ideal edge length to sphere radius.
Decagon: The ten-sided base polygon of this hemisphere.
Edge: A unique line segment in the geometric mesh; not necessarily one
wooden member.
Fold: The smaller angle between outward normals of adjacent panels.
Kerf: Material removed across the width of a saw cut. Bucking kerf affects
section-length inventory; ripping kerf affects sector recovery.
Member: One finished structural wooden part, with its physical geometry
and identity.
Panel: One independently assembled triangular frame, owning three
members.
Pinwheel: A cyclic end-to-side relationship within a panel, with each
member receiving one neighbor and terminating against another.
Radial sector: A region bounded by two radii and their circular arc; one
eighth has a forty-five-degree included angle.
Seam: A shared interface between two panels. This hemisphere has
fifty-five interior seams and ten exposed base edges.

pages.title: Glossary — the words beside the cuts
pages.text:
Stock envelope: The longitudinal extent needed to contain the physical
member before any extra process allowance.
Zome: A related form based on a zonohedral construction; it has its own
geometry and is not this spherical 2V frame.
